questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of the third wave label as a description
questions.stem: The memo's glossary warns against reading the third wave label as a precise description. Explain what the label does and does not establish about a country's political trajectory.

answer.exemplar: The label groups a set of transitions that share an outward pattern: an authoritarian order gives way to competitive elections, competitive government is consolidated, and liberal rights are extended. Used that way it is a useful shorthand for comparison. It does not establish sequence, timing or cause. Countries carrying the same label arrived by very different routes, some through negotiated pacts and some through collapse, and the label says nothing about how durable the new order proved or whether it later reversed.

questions.explanation: The label summarises a common pattern of transitions but does not establish timing, sequence or causation, and it ignores how durable the resulting order proved.
questions.hint: Ask whether the label explains why a transition happened.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why event frequencies mislead comparisons of political stability
questions.stem: Explain why a table of coup frequencies can mislead a reader who wants to compare the political stability of two countries.

answer.exemplar: A frequency table records how often seizures of power occurred, and it says nothing about the length of the periods between them. One country may show four takeovers in a single year of crisis and then fifty years without one, while another shows a single takeover followed by six decades of orderly government. Counting the events ranks the first country as more unstable even though it has been stable for half a century. Any comparison therefore needs a measure of the intervals, and ideally of how durable the settlement after each event proved, rather than the raw tallies.

questions.explanation: Tallies ignore the intervals between events, so a single burst of coups in one country can outrank another that has been stable for decades. Comparison needs duration and durability measures.
questions.hint: Ask how long the stable periods lasted.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why departing rulers prefer written guarantees to promises
questions.stem: Explain why a departing ruler may prefer written guarantees over a public promise that power will be handed over peacefully.

answer.exemplar: A public promise is easy to make and cheap to break, because the departing ruler has no leverage once he no longer holds office and no way to check whether the terms are being honoured. Written guarantees travel with him into the new order: they can be attached to the constitution, given standing before a body that cannot ignore them, and backed by international actors whose recognition the new government values. That record matters because the whole reliability of a negotiated exit rests on the new government's ability to be seen keeping it.

questions.explanation: Public promises are unenforceable once the ruler leaves office, while written guarantees create a durable record and outside stakes. The transition depends on the new government's reputation.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the promise after he leaves office.

questions.stem: Explain why a boundary commission that follows published rules can still be used to advantage a governing party.

answer.exemplar: Published rules constrain the commission without making its work politically neutral. The rules settle how districts are drawn, but they leave the commission with discretion over where to place the boundaries within the range those rules allow, and those choices determine how votes are grouped into seats. A governing party that knows the discretion it faces can campaign for the version of the map that suits it, select the commission's members through an appointment process it controls, and present the result as a technical product of neutral rules. Because every step is lawful and documented, the resulting advantage is hard to contest even where it is plainly intended.

questions.explanation: Rules bound the commission's discretion without eliminating it, and the party can shape the choices that remain. Published documentation makes the advantage defensible.
questions.hint: Ask what the rules leave to the commission's discretion.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the third wave label organises evidence without explaining it
questions.stem: Explain why the third wave label is useful for organising a literature and weak as an explanation.

answer.exemplar: As an organising device the label is valuable because it groups a large number of otherwise scattered transitions by their outward features, chiefly the move towards competitive elections, and it lets a researcher ask questions across those cases rather than case by case. As an explanation it is weak. The label is applied to transitions that arrived by very different routes, some negotiated and some following collapse, and to countries whose subsequent histories diverge sharply. Whatever produces the shared pattern must therefore operate independently of the route, and the label itself is silent on that mechanism, so it organises the evidence without explaining any of it.

questions.hint: Ask what the label leaves unexplained.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why coup counts misrepresent political stability
questions.stem: Explain why counting the number of coups in a country can mislead a reader about how stable its political order is.

answer.exemplar: The count records events without recording the intervals between them, and stability is largely a question of those intervals. A country that suffered four takeovers within a single year of crisis and then held elections without interruption for the following fifty years is counted as more unstable than one that experienced a single takeover and settled into a durable constitutional order for six decades. The reader is therefore comparing the frequency of extraordinary events with the persistence of an ordinary order, which are not the same measure. A sound comparison needs the duration of the settled periods and some account of whether the settlement after each event held.

questions.explanation: Tallies omit the intervals, so a past burst of coups can outrank a country stable for decades. Duration of the settled periods is the measure that matters.
questions.hint: Ask how long the stable periods lasted.

options.text: Written guarantees satisfy foreign lenders, who will not lend without a formal settlement
options.misconception: invents a financial condition the case does not mention

options.text: Written guarantees allow the incoming side to choose its own ministers without restriction
options.misconception: misreads guarantees as binding the incoming side's choices

questions.explanation: The point of a guarantee is a durable record that can be invoked later, whereas a promise depends on the other side's character. Written terms also bind the incoming side.
questions.hint: Ask what a written clause gives that a promise does not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a staircase diagram of lawful changes
questions.stem: Four boxes in a descending staircase appear in the memo's chart, each labelled with a legal change, ending with a box that reads the incumbent retains office. What does the staircase depict?

options.text: A sequence in which each illegal step ends with the removal of the incumbent
options.misconception: assumes illegality and removal, which the chart denies

options.text: A sequence of lawful changes that narrow discretion and leave the incumbent in place
A restoration of earlier powers, since each step returns authority to the earlier office
options.misconception: reads a descending sequence as restoring the old position

options.text: A coup staged over several years, in which each stage has been formally approved
options.misconception: relabels a legal erosion process as a seizure of power

questions.explanation: A descending staircase of legal changes ending with the incumbent still in office describes erosion through permitted steps. It shows neither illegality nor removal.
questions.hint: Read the final box of the staircase.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of publication rules on a redistricting process

stimulus.body: Before any map is adopted the commission shall publish a table showing, for every constituency in the proposed map and in the map in force, the total votes cast for each party at the most recent election and the population of each area. Any member who has served as an elected official within the previous five years is not eligible to sit on the commission.

questions.stem: Under the publishing rule, which effect on the redrawing process is best supported?

options.text: It removes any possibility of a partisan map, because every figure is made public
options.misconception: assumes transparency rules exclude partisan design

options.text: It prevents the commission from altering any district with a falling population
options.misconception: invents a population rule the text does not contain

options.text: It makes the effect of a proposed map on party fortunes visible and open to challenge
It requires the approval of every affected party before a map may be adopted
options.misconception: adds a consent requirement the rule does not impose

questions.explanation: Publishing vote and population figures for both maps exposes the consequences of the redrawing for party fortunes, which supports public challenge but does not forbid a partisan design.
questions.hint: Ask what the published table lets an observer do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Performance as a source of legitimation
questions.learningObjective: Compare changes in performance approval with changes in political trust
questions.stem: Working through the approval table in two stages. First, the memo records approval of the government's handling of the economy at 52 per cent in the first survey and 61 per cent in the second, while overall trust in government fell from 48 to 39 per cent. Second, choose the option that reports the changes correctly and interprets them.

options.text: Approval rose 9 points and trust rose 9 points, so economic performance revived confidence
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the trust series

options.text: Approval rose 9 points and trust fell 9 points, so the two survey figures cannot both be right
options.misconception: treats two differing results as evidence of data error

options.text: Approval rose 61 points and trust fell 39 points, which uses levels rather than changes
options.misconception: reports the levels instead of the changes

options.text: Approval rose 9 points while trust fell 9 points, so performance does not repair trust

questions.explanation: Every campaign with a single demand obtained it and every campaign without any demand obtained nothing, so the pattern supports an association with clarity of aim. The table records no crowd sizes.
questions.hint: Difference each pair of survey figures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Judge how widely a wave label is applied in a review table
questions.stem: The memo's table records 40 transitions. Of these, 12 are labelled third wave, 9 fall in the second wave and 19 are described as reversals or consolidations without a wave label. Which reading of the table is best supported?

options.text: The third wave label is applied to a minority of the cases the memo reviews
The third wave label is applied to the majority of transitions in the table
options.misconception: reverses the majority and minority counts

options.text: Most transitions in the period were reversals of earlier liberalisation
options.misconception: treats the unlabelled group as a single category of reversal

options.text: Wave labels have been abandoned by the review because of the reversals
options.misconception: infers abandonment from a table that still applies labels

questions.explanation: Twelve of forty is 30 per cent, so the third wave label covers a minority of the reviewed cases and the unlabelled group is the largest. The table records no abandonment of the vocabulary.
questions.hint: Compare the twelve with the total of forty.
